utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Monday the 16th of March, 2009. I would like first of all to greet the accused. I would like to greet Mr. Coric, specifically. We are happy to see that he is back in the courtroom today. I can see that Mr. Pusic has taken ill. We hope therefore that he will get better as soon as possible. I would also like to greet the counsel, Mr. Stringer and his associates, as well as all the people assisting us in this courtroom. Registrar, I believe you have four IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. OTP has submitted its objection to documents tendered by 2D via witness Tihomir Majic. This list shall be given Exhibit IC947. Two parties have submitted their list of documents to be tendered through witness Bato Hamid. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC00948. The list submitted by the Prosecution shall be given Exhibit IC 00949. 2D has submitted its list of documents to be tendered through witness Cengic Nedzad. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC00950. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Trial Chamber will hand out an oral decision, an oral decision relating to a leave to reconsider the oral decision concerning a request filed by the Prlic Defence with a view to exceeding the word count in its motion, motion relating to the provisional release of the accused Prlic. On the 2nd of March, 2009, Prlic Defence filed leave for provisional release as well as the permission to exceed the word count in this same motion. On the 9th of March, 2009, the Trial Chamber handed down an oral decision dismissing the Prlic Defence's motion to exceed the threshold of 3.000 words which is the authorised threshold. In this decision, the Trial Chamber stipulated that it was therefore for the Prlic Defence to file a new submission that would abide by the authorised number of words. On the 13th of March, 2009, the Prlic Defence filed a request to review the decision handed down by the Chamber on the 9th of March, 2009, submitting that these were exceptional circumstances. The Trial Chamber does not see that there is any exceptional circumstance that would entitle the Prlic Defence not to file a 3.000-word long motion to ask for the provisional release of the accused Prlic. The Trial Chamber therefore decides not to reconsider its decision of the 9th of March, 2009, and asks the Prlic Defence, as it has already asked it to do, to file if it so wishes a submission containing no more than 3.000 words. So in short, the Trial Chamber is awaiting another motion relating to the provisional release of the accused in question that does not exceed the 3.000 word count. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm not about to re-argue anything, however I do wish to state that the factual predicate that you've just outlined is incorrect. At least not the one that you gave us last week and not the one that I saw on the transcript. As I understood it, last time you indicated that we did not give sufficient reasoning, and -- which is why we filed for reconsideration. Had you said that categorically and under no circumstances you were going to allow anything over 3.000, I would not have wasted my time in filing for reconsideration. So I'd like the record to reflect that based on your suggestions, that's what we did. So if we are going to be summarising the facts, Mr. President, I do hope that the facts are accurately reflected each and every occasion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Unfortunately, I don't have before me the oral decision that was handed down last time, but if I remember correct finally, I believe we were very clear, I think it was unambiguous. You may be right, we will look at it again, and we will check what was said at the time. And we shall take into account what you have just mentioned, but this will be based on the transcript because I don't have the oral decision before me. Whatever the case may be, Mr. Karnavas, you may file your request for provisional release and the Trial Chamber will hand out its decision very quickly. Let's bring the witness in now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivan Bandic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a lot of interference in the courtroom, and the interpreters did not hear the date of birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your job or your current occupation? Witness, can you give me your job and current occupation, and could you give us your date of birth again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my name is Ivan Bandic. By profession I'm a lawyer, and I am a the ambassador of the Republic of Croatia in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th of November, 1959.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ambassador, have you already testified before a court of law on the facts that unfolded in the former Yugoslavia, or are you testifying for the first time today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, today I'm testifying for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may read the text of the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. Ambassador, just some brief information I'd like to give you, Your Excellency. I believe that in your capacity you know how this Tribunal operates I'm sure, and I'm sure your lawyer has briefed you. You will answer questions put to you by Ms. Nozica. She will undoubtedly show you a number of questions in support of the questions -- show you a number of documents in support of the questions she's going to put to you. This will last approximately 3 hours. The other Defence counsel will also put questions to you if at the deem it necessary adds part of their cross-examination, and they have one hour and a half all in all. After that, the Prosecutor who is sitting on your right-hand side, Mr. Stringer I believe today, will proceed with his cross-examination which will last 3 hours which is the same time as Ms. Nozica will have had. The four judges that form the Bench may intervene and put questions, particularly when documents are shown to you, and may put questions to you which they deem appropriate. Which means that your testimony should last four days this week. You are now a witness of the court since you have taken the oath, and this means that you must not contact anyone before next Thursday. But I'm sure you understand this perfectly well. Try and be as accurate as you possibly can when you answer the questions, but in your current capacity I have no concerns about this. We have a break every hour and a half to enable everyone to have a rest and we need to turn the tapes around also. If at any point in time you feel uneasy or have a problem, don't hesitate to raise your hand so that we suspend the hearing if need be. I would also like to say to Mr. Coric that if any point in time he wishes to get up during the hearing, I know that he has back problems, if he wishes to stand at any point in time, he may. And if he wishes to have a rest, this will be granted to him. This is what I had to say, and I shall now give the floor to Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And good afternoon to you, too, Mr. Bandic.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to go through your CV briefly. You needn't answer after each of my observations, but just tell me if I say something that is not correct. So you can wait until I go through your CV and then tell me afterwards. You graduated from the faculty of law in 1985?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And your first employment was in Grude municipality from 1985 to 1986?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then you were the secretary of a firm called Herzegovina Putoli [phoen], Herzegovina roads from 1986 to 1988?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From 1988 to 1991 you were in the service of the state security of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From April 1992 until the autumn of 1994, you were an employee in the SIS administration in the Security Sector of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly during that time, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From the -- around the autumn of 1984 [as interpreted] until the 1st of March, 1995, you worked in the HIS, which is the Croatian intelligence service attached to the Defence ministry of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From the 1st of March, 1995, until the 1st of March, 1997, you were an advisor to the ambassador in Sarajevo attached to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You were employed in the same area from the 1st of March 1997, until the 1st of February, 1999, in the embassy in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You worked on these same affairs from the 1st of June of 1999 until the 15th of December 2000 at the embassy in Tehrana?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You continued working in the area from the 1st of February, 2001, until the 15th of November, 2002, in the Croatian embassy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: From the 15th of November, 2002, until the 31st of December, 2006, you were the consul general or performed the duties of consul general in Pecs in the state of Hungary?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And from the 1st of January 2007 to the present day, you have been the Croatian ambassador in Hungary -- to Hungary?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, now, although we just said that during my reading out of your CV, could you tell the Trial Chamber when you worked first for the HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: My first job or my first assignment and involvement in the Croatian Defence Council was at the beginning of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And what was your job at the time? What work were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I was part of the military police of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: My superior was Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that that was in April 1992; right? How long did you stay in that post, and where did you move to after that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly between April and July of that same year, that was it, and afterwards I became employed in the security service within the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And who was your superior there within the security service?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That was Mr. Ivica Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, do you know who appointed Mr. Lucic to his positions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge it was Mr. Boban who appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I remember that it was towards the end of July 1992. Yes, the end of July, 1992 would be it. And I remember that for the simple reason that this was an important thing for me too because at that time together with Mr. Lucic I started building up the service as such, and those were the fledgling structures of the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you remember, and I'm saying this because we haven't found the document on your appointment, but can you remember which specific tasks Mr. Boban appointed Mr. Lucic, or, rather, we couldn't find Mr. Lucic's papers of appointment?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Lucic was the chief of the Security and Information Service, the SIS, or rather, the SIS administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you were engaged in first, you and Mr. Lucic? What kind of work did you do within SIS? What were your first tasks and how many employees were there, where were your premises, and so on?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the pioneer days of the service. We started -- well, the two of us started working, and we tried to find some more people to do the work involved. We needed to find the premises, and physically that was in Mostar, and briefly speaking we did what we could with the resources that we had and tried to set up the organisation from finding a table and chairs and a computer, the car, so we had to start from scratch. There were five or six of us to begin with or, rather, we managed to recruit five or six people over the next few months and start the whole ball rolling.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber which building your premises were in?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: The SIS administration from the first to the last day was at the entrance to Mostar on the left, as far as I remember, and before the war it was called the Tobacco Institute. That was the building. And nearby there was a petrol station and opposite there was the cathedral, and I'm saying that so that anybody who knows their way around will be able to understand where we were located in Mostar. And we were in the attic, up in the loft. That is to say the top of the building. Well, it wasn't really a big building. It was a house with a ground floor and two upper storeys and we were right up at the top.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was there anybody else there? Any other service located in that same building when you took up residence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, nobody had installed themselves yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, we see that this was your first involvement, and all my questions will be linked to the work you did in the SIS administration. Tell me, please, how long did you stay working in that field?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Well, I remained there until 1994. I remained within the SIS administration, and my immediate involvement was until the Washington agreement roughly, and I finished the work that I was doing there in the SIS administration or, rather, the HVO or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as I've already said at the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your specific tasks were? I'm not talking about the SIS administration, but what did you personally do? What were you personally involved with?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Well, already in the autumn of 1992, as I remember, I went out into the field and one of the first times I went was, well, memorable because it was an area in central Bosnia, I went to Kiseljak to attend negotiations there with UNPROFOR and other parties in Sarajevo, and I mention that occasion because it has embedded itself in my memory. I went together with Mr. Petkovic and another person, that first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And subsequently did you go again, and if so, could you tell the Trial Chamber roughly how much time you spent in the area until, let's say, the Washington Agreement in 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I went several times. I would say a total of five to seven months is how long I spent there. I can't be quite sure, but anyway, I went on a case-to-case basis. I would go for two or three days, but sometimes those days would stretch to two to three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who did you go with, Mr. Bandic, and in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Now, when I say that I went into the field, I mean central Bosnia mostly, and almost always that was with Mr. Petkovic. At the beginning, I think he was a colonel, but very soon after that he became a general, so I went with General Petkovic. And so in a way I was his, if I might be allowed to say so, his driver and his body-guard and his secretary and in a way his assistant. I helped him as much as I could, and whenever I went there, I was almost always with General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, what assignments did you have within the SIS administration? What jobs did you have, what tasks from the beginning of your employment there, and did things change later on? What did you do specifically?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: At the beginning when I spoke about how SIS came into being, my work was technical, evolving my professional knowledge, and now what I knew about the security system was perhaps a little more than my colleagues knew because as I've already said, I spent two or three years working in the former state in the former service, so that was the sort of groundwork of my knowledge in the security sphere. Now, as far as going into the field is concerned, my job was, as I've already said, to help General Petkovic as much as I could, and at the same time to collect information and intelligence of importance to security, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were you in any way an employee, and if so when, tell the Trial Chamber when, were you attached to the Main Staff in any way and at any time?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in the Main Staff. I cannot confirm, or, rather, I don't remember when I was served the official papers appointing me to that post, but sometime from the summer of 1993, I was in the Main Staff and physically I would be up there. First of all in Citluk, and then in Posusje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what the tasks of the SIS were? Could you please tell us how they were regulated. Was there a legal basis for that? However, basically I'm asking you as an operative what the tasks of the SIS were to the best of your understanding?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: The basic job of the service was counter-intelligence protection of the forces of the HVO and everything that pertains to this military field. So basically it was counter-intelligence protection first and foremost. Of course, it involved other work as prescribed by the rules and regulations of the security service. As far as I can remember, these rules were passed in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, were there some written rules before these rules came into force?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I think so. Part of them were regulated through the Decree on the Armed Forces, and I believe that a part was regulated through the disciplinary rules. At any rate, an effort was made throughout to create a legal framework so that the security service would have its proper place.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, can you tell me how the Security Sector was organised in the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: My knowledge in this regard was as follows: Formally, it was envisaged but it never actually started to operate, for objective and subjective reasons. However, it was my understanding that one in the same person was supposed to be, and indeed was, at the head of the security service and one of the divisions and that was the SIS administration. So it was supposed to be the military police administration and the SIS administration. It was my understanding that basically the sector never started functioning in the true essential of the word as it had been envisaged and as it was supposed to function.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please tell me first and foremost who this one person was who was suppose today head the Security Sector Administration and the SIS?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Ivica Lucic headed this Security Sector, and at the same time he headed the SIS administration. As for the military police, it was Mr. Valentin Coric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Second question stemming from this, you said that practically the Security Sector never started to function, are you talking about the entire period while you were an official in the SIS until April 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the period I'm referring to. However, I would like to add something. Towards the end of 1993, as Mr. Biskic came, he became formally, the assistant for security. He came to that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask you to explain to Their Honours how the SIS administration was organised?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said how many people were supposed to be there and what the resources were supposed to be. However, it was supposed to have it's offices, different ones, one was the operative one, the other one was the analytical one, and there was even a personnel administrative section, and that is how the SIS started functioning. As time went by, what was envisaged was to establish centres based on the territorial principle, centres of the SIS. When I say "on the territorial principle," that means they were supposed to include operative zones.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, could you please explain what the link was between the SIS administration and the centres? How was it envisaged, although as you said they were supposed to start functioning as time went by, and we'll see whether they actually did, but what is your understanding? What was the link supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: In a way, SIS centres were supposed to be a link between the SIS in the military districts, in the units, that is, and towards the administration. At any rate, it was supposed to provide for professional assistance for members of the service who were in the centres and further down in the units, from battalion and brigade level, lower than that, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, can you explain to the Trial Chamber how -- or rather, when you started working on this job, what was your relationship like with these members of units who were in charge of SIS, did they start working on this before your appointment, and, generally speaking, what kind of link existed between you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Centres did try to establish this link. Unfortunately it was very difficult. The military police, as I already mentioned, was established in the beginning of April. At the same time, units were established as well, and in these units, of course, there were people who represented the SIS. Practically, that means that a few months after the administration started functioning, we had a situation involving people who were already in the units and already did represent the SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was your communication like with them? On what basis could you give them assignments and what was this communication between the administration or, rather, centres and the members of the SIS in the respective units, the assistant commanders and other officers in the units?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Communication was very difficult. Virtually impossible. This was another one of the reasons why we made an effort to establish the centres, and may I repeat once again, they practically never started operating in the full sense of the word. There were people who, from an educational and professional point of view, and even security related and moral point of view who -- these were people who were simply not supposed to be there. But this was dictated by the actual situation as it was in the field, where battalion and brigade commanders quite simply decided on their own who they would appoint to these positions. That is to say, well, quite simply this was left to individuals and their arbitrary decisions, who would hold these positions. While we are on the subject, I have to tell you that brigades in certain municipalities were established in the following way: The municipality, or rather, every municipality was a state per se and the brigade was the armed force of this state, conditionally speaking. So it was very troublesome to have any kind of communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first binder in front of you, and now, in relation to this establishment, I should like to point out that I'm going to put a few questions to you and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Excellency, you just mentioned something that I feel is particularly important but you said it very quickly, and if I may, I'd like to come back to that particular issue. It's on page 16, line 8 and following. You say, and I quote: "The municipalities worked as a state, and the brigades that had been set up by the municipalities seemed to see themselves as an armed force of that particular municipality." Could you perhaps give us more accurate details on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge and to the best of my ability, I can say that the times were very chaotic then, and I apologise for using that term. Most of this was rather spontaneous. When I say that, I'm saying that the municipalities behaved in this way. Quite simply, I see that this was inherited from the times of the previous state where indeed municipalities were independent units where they had, in peacetime, I mean, their own Territorial Defence. And unfortunately, a lot of this behaviour continued during the war. Many heads of municipalities behaved as if this were, conditionally speaking of course, their brigade, their army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you perhaps give us an example of one municipality or several municipalities that match the scheme you indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Grude, the municipality that I was born in, was based on that principle. I don't know after how many months, but after the administration was established, I came across a man in Grude who represented -- introduced himself, rather, as a SIS officer of the brigade and as the commander of the brigade, and the establishment of the brigade itself depended on the local authorities to a very large extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, may I continue in respect to this question. For example, as far as Neum and Capljina are concerned, did you have any information from your own line of work or generally speaking that that's how things functioned in an identical way, Ljubuski, other places?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I had just wanted to tell the Honourable Trial Chamber about the example that I saw with my own eyes in my own municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In line 22, I mentioned Ljubuski -- sorry, I actually said "Capljina" and it doesn't seem to be recorded. However, you said that you wanted to proceed from your own municipality. So if you found the binder, I started telling you, it seems that there's no way of having Capljina on the record. Oh yes, it is there now, thank you. Sorry about that. You said -- or, rather, I said that I would ask you about this particular section now. I'm going to point that out each and every time. Now I'm going to ask you about the establishment of the SIS, and that's going to be the next few documents. The first document I would like you to look at is 2D1333. It should be the first one in your binder.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: "Mr. Boban hearby appoints Mr. Valentin Coric on the 13th of April, 1992, as assistant commander for the security information service." And it says that: "All Croatian Defence Council military police units should also come under his command." Were you engaged in the military at that time when Mr. Coric was your superior?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P00615. Can we please have a look at that now?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what was the document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: P00615. I'll take things in the right order, and if I skip something, I'll point it out. This is a decision and the appointment of Mr. Lucic. It is stated here that he is appointed assistant head of the Defence Department for security, the date is the 21st of October, 1992. I pointed out, and I would like to point out once again, that we do not have his appointment to the SIS administration as he was appointed by Mr. Boban. Can you confirm that at the time Mr. Ivica Lucic was appointed assistant head of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's one in the same person. I would like to point out once again that it was the end of October -- or, rather, July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, since we spoke of the tasks of the SIS --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Ms. Nozica because of all the background noise apparently coming from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking us to speak a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: No, we cannot hear due to background noise. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Your response to the previous question, when I asked you whether you knew that Mr. Lucic had been appointed the assistant head of security, what was that answer?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I would like to ask to you look at document P00588. This is a Decree on the Armed Forces which was passed on the 17th of October, 1992. I would like us to look at page 137, or, rather, Article 137, which is the only one referring to the tasks of the SIS. 137. The page is 22. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Article 137 says: "Professional work in the armed forces and in the Defence Department will be carried out by the SIS." Mr. Bandic, would that be the right definition in your mind of the basic work that you were supposed to carry out within the SIS administration?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be it roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In this article it says that there is a commission that carries out this work which is appointed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Do you remember whether this commission for checking the work of the SIS was ever established?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Document P858, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we were talking about Article 137, we just saw it. This article, I must admit, leaves me perplexed, perhaps because it is fairly imprecise and since you were a member of that service, you may be able to shed some light on it. When I read this article, I feel that members of the SIS, and you were one of them, had two missions in fact, classical missions, those of a secret services and security missions. When I look at this article, I see that the work, that is intelligence work, is apparently supervised by a committee that is appointed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna following a proposal by the chief of the Defence Department. This is a traditional structure in democratic states where intelligence services are controlled by an authority which could be a committee, as is the case in this particular instance. However, when we look at the end of the article, we see that reference, clear reference is made to the military police which is in charge of security. Now, apparently this seems to be general security, so military traffic, military order, military discipline, and also procedures relating to infringements committed within the arms forces. And therefore, we feel that two entities are juxtaposed relating to security, the military police playing a part with the SIS, and then regarding what we call intelligence, the SIS in that case is competent, but we also see that within the brigades there is also -- there are also members who are members of the SIS. So is that what this article is telling us, and is that what you personally saw happening on the ground, the way this Article 137 was being implemented? It's either a general article or it isn't. Is it a general article and then on the ground it didn't quite happen like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try and explain that to the best of my ability. When these documents were passed, they were necessary because there was an attempt, probably for the best intentions, to establish these organs, and so many of these regulations were copied from the former services of the former state as you said, as they would be in peacetime, and I think to this day the same thing happens in similar fashion. But the situation at that time and in that area was completely different, of course. And as you yourself mentioned, in the units themselves there were people from SIS just as there were people from the military police. The endeavours made were geared towards having this system built up and linked up as much as possible. And let me emphasise once again that this was a very difficult thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you confirm that within the units there was the military police but also elements from the SIS, but those two entities, were they controlled by the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. That's quite right, Your Honour. They were subordinated to the commanders of battalions through the brigade up until the military district level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour asked you about the control exercised and he mentioned one of the mechanisms that were applied in every democratic country, and as far as I know every democratic country does have a service of this kind, and you said a moment ago that as far as you know the control commission or the organ that was in control and supervised was not established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's now look at P858, please. That's the next document. And tell me when you've found it. It's the next document in your binder. This is a proposal by Mr. Bruno Stojic in conformity with Article 137 of the decree to appoint the commission for controlling the work of the Security and Information Service. Can you confirm that you never heard that this commission actually ever took effect or was appointed by Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've never seen this document before, or, rather, I've never heard about this commission, although the individuals listed from 1 to 5, I know some of them personally, but I am not aware of any commission having ever been formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go and discuss the interior organisation of the Security Sector. And you've already told the Judge that the provisions were written in the way they were written, but let's just have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All this is going very fast, but the Trial Chamber has been working on these issues 24 hours a day for three years, so every time there is a document we try and establish a link between the document and fundamental questions. And I see that this document which you say you don't know was -- dates the 3rd of December, 1992, by Mr. Bruno Stojic who is head of the department. And apparently, commission is being set up for the control of the SIS. And what I notice here is that amongst the members of the commission there are presidents of the municipalities. There are at least five of them. Well, three presidents and two deputy presidents or vice-presidents. But we see when we read these documents that municipalities seem to play a part in the political and administrative life and, possibly, also in the field of intelligence, in the field of the army. How do you explain, sir, the fact that you take the president of Livno, Siroki Brijeg, and of that municipality of Derventa, and that they are called upon in order to control the activity carried out by the intelligence service. Do you have any explanation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my position and the post I occupied quite simply did not give me scope for that kind of information. All I can do is comment. I can only say what I saw on the ground, in the field when I went around the area. And that is to say that the presidents of the municipalities or, rather, the municipal HVOs endeavoured to have and did have a firm position, and that was particularly true in 1992 because I didn't know that the commission ever existed. So that's one thing. And the second point is that this document at that time, or after all that time, well, I never knew of the existence of this particular document. And let me repeat again, I never knew that such a commission was ever established.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's try and explain that. This is a proposal to form a commission and that's what it says. It says "Subject: Proposal to appoint a commission," sent to Mr. Boban, and the witness said that he never heard of any such commission being set up, so that's what I want to clarify. This was a proposal, and we have no witnesses, this one or any of the others, who can confirm that the commission ever came into being.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's try and pin-point where the Security Sector was within the Defence Department. Look at P00586, the next document, please. Have you found it? Yes, it's the decision on the basic premises for the establishment of the Defence Department signed by a Mr. Boban on the 15th of September, 1992, and I'd like to ask you to look at point 5 of that decision on the basic principles of organisation of the Defence Department. You said how the Security Sector was envisaged. It says assistant for the Security Sector is responsible for the work of the Security Sector, and under that we have the SIS administration and the military police administration. And it says, the deputy head for security shall also perform the duties of chief of the security administration. Now, Mr. Bandic, is that how things were established as it says?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I've already said that that's how things were supposed to be, but in actual fact they never ever came into being that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's look at the following decision, the number of which is 2D567. It's the decision on internal organisation, and the date we have there, it is signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, the agreement is given by Mr. Boban, and I'd like to ask you to look at point 4. And it says the Security Sector, relations within this sector are separately defined, and it says assistant head for analytical affairs and assistant head for operative affairs in the security information service is appointed by the head of the Defence Department on proposals made by the assistant head for security. Now, you confirm that within the frameworks of SIS, analytical affairs existed and operative affairs as separate segments, separate sections; right? Within SIS, within the SIS administration.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, then we have all the heads of centres listed, and it says that they are appointed by the head of the Defence Department based on proposals from the assistant head of security. Now, do we have an assistant head of security in the commands of the operative zones? Yes, we do. Then we can read the brigades lower down. The heads of the Defence Department had proposals by -- made by the security man, and then it says all the other operative and workers in the Security Sector shall be deployed by the assistant head along with previous agreement from the head of the Defence Department or the individual that he authorises. Now, I have two questions for you. Were you one of those operatives who were supposed to be appointed by Mr. Lucic in agreement with the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And secondly, the heads of the commands of security in the operative zones and the brigades in your opinion, and you've already spoken about this, were they appointed in the way that is set out here and provided for by this document, that is to say, by the head at the proposal of the assistant head?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know whether this procedure was respected and put into practice?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: No, because I've explained to you that we came across a situation as it was and that is because the HVO started to be formed in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Bandic, we have the next document which is P2477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bandic, when you answered Ms. Nozica's question, you have just confirmed the following: You were in charge of operational activities, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was in the operative sector or operations sector of the SIS administration, and that was one of the three departments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me put to you a question now regarding the operational sector. Perhaps this is not relevant, but let me ask you this: Did you conduct any secret operations, undercover operations like tapping your opponent's telephone lines and tapping friend's lines perhaps even, and you prepared very confidential reports which you then gave Mr. Boban? Is that how things happen, like things happen in the intelligence services in other countries, democratic countries also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time and throughout the time that I was in SIS we simply did not have the technical facilities when you are talking about tapping and interception. We didn't have trained people. Nor did we have the technical devices to tap into phone lines. And I personally was not able to provide any information to Mr. Boban. When I say the operations department, that was me, and then later on two or three other people joined. So we tried, as best as we could, to train and educate people to provide them with basic knowledge about security and security related issues. And let me stress once again, the SIS as the military counter-intelligence service. Counter-intelligence service is what I would like to emphasise here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had you had the appropriate equipment and the right staff, would you have conducted such an operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our work, that part was not envisaged at all. We quite simply didn't have the authority for anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand properly, inside the HVO no one did any in-depth intelligence work like this is usually conducted? In other words, nobody was doing this kind of job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, within the frameworks of the intelligence system, there was the military intelligence service and that was its task. Pure intelligence work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, it was a military intelligence department that was involved in this, this is what you've just said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I want to say is this, along with SIS as the counter-intelligence service, there was the military intelligence service as well alongside it, and if I might be allowed to describe our work, it was this: Our work went up to the frontlines where the HVO forces were, whereas the intelligence part was across the front-line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, and I apologise to the witness. I would just like to draw your attention to the interpretation of the military intelligence service, which seems to be incorrect, so then this might lead to misunderstanding and the understanding of the security service and SIS on the one hand, and the military intelligence service of -- was on the other which was under the Main Staff, VRS. Now, this military intelligence service on the previous page in lines 9 to 16 was translated as the military intelligence service. It's not intelligence, as opposed to the informative and security system which is intelligence. So just to differentiate between the two services, I think that the witness said it correctly, but I don't think it was interpreted correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, do you agree with what Ms. Alaburic has just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree. That was the correct way it should read.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, when we are talking about the tappings in service and when we come to the provisions of the work of the information service - and we'll come to that quite soon - and ask questions with respect to intercepts and tapping, we'll do that in due course, but please look at P2477 first now, please. And for the record, let's just say, Mr. Bandic, that it is the decision on the internal establishment of the 20th of May, 1993, regulating this area when it comes to the Security Sector, or, rather, the SIS administration so that we have no need to deal with that. Now, I'd like to ask you to look at document 2D924. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is basically a diagram of the Security Sector. Since you said what you said about the Security Sector, I would now just like to deal with the SIS administration. Does this schematic, this diagram, at least basically show what did exist along the first line, analysis, the chief and the operations and work methodology desk?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: In operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Operations?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Roughly, how many people worked in operations, say from the beginning of its work until mid-April 1994?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Madam, are you referring to the entire administration or only operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Only operations this time. You've already said it but --

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, well, it was a maximum of five people. Up to five people.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Down here we see SIS centres for southeastern Herzegovina, Mostar, Tomislavgrad, Travnik, Derventa, respectively. Tomislavgrad, Travnik, Derventa. To the best of your recollection, were these centres actually established, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the setup that we see was the one that was envisaged. However, as far as the centres are concerned, I can testify that up to the very end they never started fully functioning. Apart from these centres we had also intended, due to the situation that we had -- rather, there were many enclaves in the territory. We even wanted to have sub-centres as lower ranking establishments. However, this was carried out on paper only. Not in real life.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Now we are going to deal with the number of engaged persons in the SIS, so I'd like to ask you to look at 2D931. This is sort of halfway down the period while you were working there, and this is the payroll for May 1993, and we see that the total number of employees is as it is here, and we see the Mostar centre of the SIS, there's only 13 people. Then the Mostar SIS centre and the Travnik SIS centre. We will deal with this centre a bit later, and we will use it as an example of the work that was being done, and I would just like to draw your attention to what it says here. That it was from the HVO Grude that you got your salaries in May 1993. Can you comment on this? Does that mean that there were municipalities that had resources for salaries and that the department did not have enough money to pay salaries to its employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I do apologise. I agree, yes. I agree. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please explain -- let me rephrase my question now -- to the best of your knowledge, if you do know, why is there this note here, why does it say from the HVO of Grude we got 13.125.000 Croatian Dinars for salaries?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my explanation of this is as follows: This is the place where I was born. And in Grude there was this logistics centre. Grude, in a way, conditionally speaking was a centre. It was the centre of the Croatian Community. Obviously, the municipality of Grude had enough money on its bank account and had the ability to help financially at that point in time. However, yet again I would like to draw your attention to what I've already said, that the local communities, in this case the municipalities, had great power in certain situations of course. Madam, as far as personnel are concerned, this was the number that changed a bit, perhaps it went up by 10 at a maximum, so that is the number of SIS members in the administration and at the centres. Of course, I know practically all of these people personally, this includes drivers, secretaries, typists, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell me in the SIS administration, now that we are looking at this document, that is the first column. Objectively speaking, how many operatives were there and when do the technical personnel start or end?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: I can say that these are three persons including myself, yours truly, we were in charge of operations, operative work in a way.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next document. We are just going to look at the number of employees briefly. 2D939. This is the payroll for October 1993. The previous one was for July. Can we state that there are 34 on this list as well; right? We can see the names and they are the same people, aren't they, Mr. Bandic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Well, practically it's an identical list. Maybe only a few names changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us look at November, 2D947. This is a document that is called the method of financing the work of the service. But could you please look at the last page, and on the last page we have the number of employed persons, the number of officials, and it says here 35, 34, 40, and 60. Does this roughly correspond to your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Indeed. I don't know this number, I mean, 60, well, to the best of my knowledge, and I did have direct knowledge, I don't know how it grew to this figure. I think that around 40 would have been a realistic number, or, rather, the number of people I came across there. Of course, I do allow for the possibility that there were 60 there, but I don't know who was quite simply attached.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, we'll get to these questions when we get to the rules and to the re-organisation of the service and the establishment of centres. However, except for this number that seems excessive to you, otherwise this does correspond to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please look at document -- I would like to thank the interpreters. So far I had the feeling that I haven't been hurrying too much and that we were working well. It's my fault for rushing. 2D944 is the next document I would like you to look at. This is a list of officials signed by Mr. Ivica Lucic. 19th of November, 1993, is the date. This is a list of HVO units and SIS officials within them. And it says here Main Staff, number 1 command Ivan Bandic, chief SIS officer; and Predrag Covic, SIS officer. Was that the time when you were working there and tell me who was there attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, yes, that is the time when physically and formally -- I see that right now. Although, allow me to note something, I don't know what this word "Glavni" pertains to. I think it should have said SIS officer at the Main Staff, because if it says chief SIS officer, Glavni, I don't know who the one that was not the chief one would be. So I really don't know what this word would mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us just look at page 7, that's a list of all officers. In English it would be page number 8. So could we please have that, and I would like us to look at a particular note here. It's towards the end of your page. It says Mostar, and then 1, 2, and then there is something underneath number 2, Zarko Pavlovic was replaced, however he is a strong negative personality in the brigade and is obstructing its dismissal, so practically the dismissal is still underway. It say that is Raguz was proposed by the brigade commander, Obradovic, who would be a suitable person, and Raguz was supposed to propose a SIS officer in the brigade. Now, we are just giving this as an example of appointments and coordination on the basis of what we have seen. Mr. Zarko Pavlovic, as stated here, it says the dismissal is underway, the replacement is underway, was he ever actually replaced to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge this was never carried through. May I add something, there were a few such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you to look at the last page, it's the last page in the Croatian and in the English and that is the note in relation to this list. Most of the SIS officers in units, zones, brigades, battalions, and MTD were appointed in contravention of the existing decision made by the Defence Department, so there are no legal possibilities. The procedure is such -- is that the chief should propose SIS officers for a particular place -- for particular positions, however this procedure was violated in the following way. Commanders of the brigades were appointing SIS officers without asking the assistant minister of security for his approval. Mr. Bandic, do you remember this? This is already in November, and you said that your administration started working in July, 1992, this is November 1993. Do you remember that all this time there was this resistance to having this established as envisaged by the rules in.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. That was the situation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We have two proposals here. And it says that there should be an assessment of all SIS personnel to date, and then there should be new appointments. So let's look at the next document that has to do with this, 2D949.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that we will manage to finish with this document, and then we can take the break. 949.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, this is a document dated the 22nd of November, 1993. According to the very logic of things, it is a continuation of the previous document. Again it's signed by Ivica Lucic, and as we can see he is sending it to Mr. Biskic, who was then already appointed assistant minister in the Security Sector; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It says, Here on the basis of your order we submit to you the following: Names of employees of the SIS who have been appointed to establishment post who are satisfactory workers and should be retained in the service; names of SIS employees who have not been appointed to establishment post but who are satisfactory workers and should be retained in the service; names of SIS centre employees who can no longer work in the service; and lists of all other employees who are not included in the above lists and who do not have the approval of this Security Sector, who do not possess a decision on appointment. It says here, A decision on their future status in this service should be made. On the next page is a list of SIS officers who do not have an appointment decision, and you're the first one there. But it says here that your work is satisfactory, all six of you, and that you should stay on the job, and it says here that you are attached to the Main Staff, and yet again, number 6, Predrag Covic. Can you confirm that at the time you did not have appointment decisions in terms of this particular post as stated here?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, and Your Honours, if I may just briefly. A year and a half after the administration was established, an attempt was made to bring things in order, to deal with the situation as it was. A list of was made here of persons who were within the SIS. Once again, I would like to point out that there were these slip, if I can put it this way. In one document it says that I was chief SIS officer, and this one it says specifically that I was the SIS officer at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: One more question in relation to this document and then the break. Please look at the last page. It is very indicative. Let us comment on this. List of employees according to units with appointments made by the SIS. Mr. Bandic, there are 15 names here, so they were appointed by the administration, and this was legal as envisaged. Can you confirm, and we've been counting this 15 people, only 9 assistants, only 9 assistants who were supposed to be established in terms of this internal setup. So they were elected or appointed according to procedure envisaged by law?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I assume that we should take the break now so I could pause.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there are a few things that I need to mention. The Registrar had a number to mention because a mistake was made.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 2D has submitted their response to Prosecution's objection to the documents tendered through witness Dragan Pinjuh. This response shall be given Exhibit IC00951. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Thank you for this correction. Now, regarding the time, Ms. Nozica, you used up an hour, 55 minutes to be precise, so you still have about 2 hours and 2 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To Mr. Karnavas, I would like to remind you of the oral decision regarding the presentation of the request for provisional release, and I would like to mention a line on the transcript, it is page 37803, at the end of the -- they are the first two lines, and I quote: "It is up to Prlic's Defence team to present a new submission respecting the limit of the word count." So the Trial Chamber does not deem this criticism by Mr. Karnavas to be justified where he said that he was surprised by this new decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if we look at the entire exchange, Your Honour, and I don't wish to get into debate. I understand that on occasion you seem to take a dim view of what I do in court, and make no bones about it, but if we look at the overall tenner as I indicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it seems to me that you are starting to argue again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This sentence is to be found, and I think that's quite enough to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- make the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You have to look at, Your Honour, the entire oral decision, and when you look at the entire oral decision, we were left with the impression, rightly or wrongly, that what motivated the Trial Chamber were two things. One was that we did not follow the proper procedure, at which point I had to point out to the Trial Chamber that the procedure that I thought -- that I used was one that was universally applied throughout this Tribunal. Well before you, Judge Trechsel, arrived here. So that was one point. The other point, when looking at the language, it appeared that the Trial Chamber was not sufficiently satisfied with explanations that we provided, so when you look at the leave that we filed again, we go out of our way to provide additional explanations why the leave was necessary. Had we -- had we known that the Trial Chamber categorically, in this instance as opposed to others where people stand up and ask orally for extension of leave and within a matter of second its granted, had we known that you had already made up your minds, I would not have wasted my time. It does take a little bit of time to put a motion together. So while you read out that one sentence, and I saw the sentence, if you look at the entire oral decision in its entirety and the way it was presented, we were left with the impression: That one, the Trial Chamber was once again not amused with Karnavas's approach, being a recidivist, at which point I have to point out that I was not doing nothing wrong; and number two, that I had not provided sufficient reasoning which is why we provided the reasoning. That's what we were left to understand, and that's why I am a bit combative at this point. Because on one hand, you question why isn't Mr. Prlic here, and on the other hand we see this going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Trial Chamber reminded you of its decision of the 2nd of March. Maybe you interpreted this decision the way you did, but as far as we're concerned, there was no -- it wasn't necessary to object to it. As far as we are concerned, the Trial Chamber decided that pursuant to the oral decision, we had invited you to present a new request, word count 3.000 words, as I had indicated earlier. So we will carry on with the examination-in-chief and I'll give you the floor, Mrs. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, staying with the same topic, that is to say establishment and organisation, and for that would you look at the next document which is P4756. These are minutes from the Chiefs of Staff meeting held on 2nd of September, 1993, or from the board meeting of heads of the Defence Department. Let me first ask you, did you attend any of those meetings, those board meetings?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's see whether you know about what it says in the minutes on page 2.2 of the Croatian and it's page 3 of the English, where it states that the book of rules and regulations governing the work and organisation of the security of information service. It says in his introduction, Mr. Lucic outlined the contents of the book of rules and regulations, the organisation of the service itself. He gives special emphasis to the work methods and the competencies of the service as specified in the book of rules and regulations. We'll deal with those rules and regulations in awhile, but here we can see that at the board meeting this was a subject that was discussed. And now I'm interested in the second observation that follows. It says, He also pointed out that he has encountered problems concerning appointments of SIS officials at brigade level. That had not been -- and that he had not been consulted about that. This, he said, would not happen again because the decision on the establishment of the Defence Department regulates how officials are to be appointed. Now, Mr. Bandic, this meeting was held, or rather, the board meeting was held on the 2nd of September, 1993, and we have seen documents dating to the end of November 1993. Can you confirm that this practice, at least up until then, was not changed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Throughout efforts were made to have this system take effect, but as we can see one year on there were still a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, take a look at the next document, please, which 2D930. And it is an order from Minister Perica Jukic on the 23rd of November, 1993, and he refers to the decision on the internal establishment of the Defence Department, as stipulated in paragraph 1, and in the second paragraph it says, With the analysis of the situation in SIS it was determined that a great number of officers of SIS and was not appointed based on the procedure, but the commanders of the HVO formations appointed the assistant for security on their own initiative. And in that regard, he is issuing the following order: That the situation should be dealt with by the 26th of November, 1993, and afterwards that appointments should be made in keeping with the regulations. Now, does this exhibit show, Mr. Bandic, that in actual fact the problem continued to exist?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, can you reformulate?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll do that. Yes, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, does this mean, or does it follow from this document that the problem continued to exist?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that does confirm that, and let me emphasise that once again we faced that problem until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We are now going to go through three more documents, Mr. Bandic, and you said that the units had assistant commanders for SIS. And look at 2D927 first, please in that regard. It is a schematic for the operative zone command. Well, it's identical in the English and Croatian, and if you look at positions 16 and 17 now, please, which is to be found -- well, there are no page numbers but anyway, 16 and 17, it says, Assistant commander for SIS and the clerk for SIS. Now, are those the individuals that held those posts in the operative zone?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now look at document 2D1370. Page 2 of the Croatian, and page 4 of the English. And this is a schematic for the brigade formation. We have that diagram. And on page 2 of the Croatian and page 4 of the English, we have the security and information department in the brigade where we have the head of SIS and the SIS desk officer. Does that correspond to the situation as you know it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now let's look at document P566. It's on page 2, and it's the diagram of the war formation of a battalion. It's page 2 in both the English and the Croatian. And it speaks of the battalion commander, under number 5, the officer for information security. So is that the person who was in charge of SIS in the battalion, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bandic, we are going to move on and look at a number of other documents and deal with questions related to the legal frameworks of the method of work for the Security and Information Service. And in order to do that, would you please look at document P4211. These are rules of procedure on the work of the information and security service. It says Mostar, August, 1993, at the bottom there. And from the document that we looked at a moment ago, which was the board meeting of the Defence Department, dated the 2nd of September, 1993, it is document P4756. You don't have to look for it again, I'm just saying that for the record. Anyway, we see that these rules were discussed and that they were enacted at this board meeting. So can you confirm that this is the first set of rules of procedure dealing with the information and security service.

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, those are the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I have already asked you this, but let's repeat it because it's important. Were there rules and regulations governing SIS before these rules of procedure were passed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fine. Now, let's start with Article 7 of these rules of procedure, which states that the professional business of the country's defence concerning the armed forces is done by the Security and Information - SIS - Service. So is that almost identical to Article or para 1 of Article 137 governing the armed forces which we saw earlier on today?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, take a look at Article 9, and may we have your comments. Does that -- does Article 9 describe the tasks that the Information and Security Service dealt with. Article 9?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it. And the emphasis is laid on counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And security protection of the Defence Department in the broader sense, that's what it says, isn't it; right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This article, in actual fact, gives the broadest definition of what the Security and Information Service should do, it's remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Judge Antonetti asked you about interception and tapping, and as far as I understood it you said you didn't have the technical resources to do that and that you didn't have the authority, either. Now, let's look at Article 42 of these rules of procedure for us to see whether that might have perhaps been regulated by these rules. Mr. Bandic, you can answer that in two ways. Here we see that it was regulated, and I was -- I'm going to ask you whether that was in fact what was done in practice. Was that translated into practice ever?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: In my introduction, I said that many documents dating back to this period were copied from earlier documents. Now, the situation on the ground was completely different.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that the SIS didn't deal in these matters, is that how I'm to understand what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: Yes. While I was there, in my time, the SIS didn't deal in these matters. And I said because of a lack of resources and a lack of manpower, we didn't have the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Bandic, I'm now going to put a hypothetical to you. You are a man of great experience in this field. A service of this kind, even if it did have the resources and manpower, could they in fact tap into conversations conducted by civilians, even if it did have the facilities to do? So I'm asking you a hypothetical question, could it intercept civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVAN BANDIC
utterances.text: No, no, it had no legal grounds for that. There were civilian intelligence services for that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'd like to ask you to look at the provisions starting out with Article 57 and ending with Article 67 which regulate mutual relations of the persons working in the administration, the SIS centres, and the assistant commanders in the units. I'm not going to spend too much time on that. I'm going to ask you more about how things stood in practice, although each article would merit explanations. But for the moment we are going to see what this looked like in practice. And in order to do that, would you please take a look at the next document, which is P592.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on to the next document in the line of questioning by Ms. Nozica about the tapping, I would invite you to look at Article 15 of the documents. Article 15 mentions the scope of your activities, what your service is meant to be doing. And I notice two main elements. First of all, you have to identify the KOS agents, the ex-JNA, and particularly those who are still in liaison with the Serbian security services, and underneath, you also have -- give information on people who are in contact with the foreign secret services. So these are traditional tasks. And then if you move on to the next page, you see that you are meant to give information on war crime. So there are many tasks. Some of them requiring intelligence operations in the traditional sense of the word, tapping and intercepts as provided for by Article 42. And you say, No, we didn't do any of this. If that is true, you confirm that you haven't done it, but then you wouldn't have been in a position to implement what Article 15 requires of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, what is listed here, as you noticed full well, is the area of responsibility of the military security information service. And this is quite literally copied from many other regulations.
